title: Brother Lawrence's kitchen
hook: a monastery cook found God as near among the pots as at the altar

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dark night, John of the Cross's season when God feels far. Your line was dark is not absent. Did it help on a flat day? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

Picture a busy kitchen at dinner time. Pots boiling over. Somebody shouting for more bread. Somebody else wants the salt. The floor is wet, the oven is too hot, and you have a limp and a bad back. Not exactly a holy place. In the 1600s, in a monastery in Paris, the cook was a clumsy former soldier who, by his own account, had a natural dislike of kitchen work. And yet visitors came away saying he was the most peaceful person they'd ever met. He said he felt God as near among the pots as in church. Today's word: practice of the presence.
screen: `POTS BOILING OVER.` → `A CLUMSY FORMER SOLDIER.` → `AS NEAR AS IN CHURCH.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicolas Herman. He grew up poor in France and became a soldier during a long and brutal war, and was wounded. The story he told later was that his faith first woke up at eighteen, looking at a bare tree in winter. He thought: soon it will have leaves again, and flowers, and fruit. And he felt, all at once, the goodness and care of God. Years later he joined the Carmelites in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Brother Lawrence. They put him in the kitchen, where he worked for many years. Later, when his leg got worse, he repaired sandals. He never wrote a book. After he died, a friend gathered his few letters and the notes of their conversations into a little collection, The Practice of the Presence of God. Its idea is simple. Talk to God all day long, in ordinary moments, in your own plain words. Not only in set times of prayer, but while you work. When you wander off, which you will, just come back, without fuss. He said that the time of work was not different to him from the time of prayer, and that in the noise and clatter of the kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, he felt God as calmly as if he were kneeling at the altar. He even said he turned his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. And when he'd finished, if there was nothing else to do, he'd pick up a straw from the floor for love of God. That's it. Nothing heroic. Just every small thing, done with God, in the room.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `A LAY BROTHER IN THE KITCHEN.` · `TALK TO GOD ALL DAY.` · `THE OMELET, FOR LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash dishes as prayer. If you're near a sink, you can do this for real. If not, picture it. The warm water, the soap, one plate at a time. With each dish, just be aware you're not alone. If you pray, you can say a word or two to God, plainly, the way you'd talk to someone standing beside you. If you don't, just give full attention to one plate. The bell holds the time.
Practice of the presence. Brother Lawrence's way: turning to God in every ordinary moment, even at the stove.
Your line: god among the pots. Today, pick one chore you don't like, and do it slowly, with God in the room. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant alike, read Brother Lawrence and try to turn to God briefly and often through the day, especially during chores and ordinary work.

fork.setup: you're praying in the kitchen and realize your mind wandered ten minutes ago. what does Brother Lawrence say to do?
options: come back to God simply, without fuss.
fork.reveal: wandering is normal. you just turn back, plainly, and go on turning the omelet.

original.note: French: the presence of God, from the title of the little book.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy people pray in churches, not kitchens.
what it means: turning to God in every small task, again and again, until work and prayer are the same thing.
what a scholar hears: a Discalced Carmelite lay brother; the book compiled after his death from letters and conversations; and prayer as simple, continual conversation.
